atoms.b: My name is Archimedes: a famous ancient ((++Greek Egyptian)) mathematician. Among other things, I was fascinated by the power of ((++levers beavers)).
atoms.sound: My name is Arkimeedees: a famous ancient Greek mathematician. Among other things, I was fascinated by the power of levers.

atoms.b: I famously once said that if you gave me a ((++lever weaver)) long enough and a ((++pivot pizza)) on which to place it, I could move the world.
Wow! I wonder if the ((++length colour)) of a lever really does make that much difference. I should find out!
atoms.sound: ssml: <prosody pitch = '-1st'>Wow! I wonder if the length of a lever really does make that much difference. I should find out!</prosody>

instruction.text: Noah has set up a lever, pivot and load. Put the steps of Noah’s experiment in order.

atoms.text: First, Noah will measure a distance between the pivot and the planned point of effort.
He will then place heavy objects at the point of effort.
When the lever is evenly balanced, Noah will record how much force was required to do so.
Noah will repeat this process, changing the distance each time.

instruction.text: Which heavy objects would be the best choice for the experiment?
Why are these the better option?

correct.text: Because he knows the exact mass of each weight, Noah can work out how much force they exert. For example, a 1kg weight exerts a force of around 10N.
correct.sound: Because he knows the exact mass of each weight, Noah can work out how much force they exert. For example, a 1kg weight exerts a force of around 10 Newtons.

instruction.text: Drag the weight to the point of effort to begin Noah’s experiment.
Look at the image and fill in Noah’s table.

instruction.text: Noah has charted his results on a graph. Answer the following questions.

atoms.a: For a distance of 10cm, how much force was needed to balance the lever?
For a distance of 70cm, how much force was needed to balance the lever?
Do these findings support the idea that longer levers require less force to lift a load?
